title: The morning brightness
hookLine: by the morning light, your Lord has not forsaken you (Quran 93)
tomorrow: one line comes back again and again in one surah. which line?

lines: HE HAS LEFT YOU, SHE SAYS.
cards: Left on read: a message delivered, seen, and then nothing, for days. There's an old story about a silence like that.

A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says the Prophet fell ill and didn't rise for the night prayer for some nights. And a woman came and mocked him: whatever spirit used to come to you, she said, has left you.
Which is yesterday's question: what if the silence goes on, and it looks like you've been left?

teach.h: BY THE MORNING, BY THE STILL NIGHT.
teach.b: The answer, in that report, is Surah ad-Duha, the Morning Brightness. It opens with two oaths, by the morning hours and by the still night, and then: "Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee."
Then it reminds him of his own life. Didn't He find you an orphan and give you shelter? Find you wandering and guide you?
Find you in need and enrich you? Then it turns outward: so the orphan, don't oppress; the one who asks, don't drive away; and of your Lord's kindness, speak.
In this surah, the comfort of not being forsaken becomes a duty to whoever might feel forsaken.

teach.h: THEN: THE ORPHAN, THE ONE WHO ASKS.
teach.b: And the night is in the oath too; some readers hear in that a sign that the quiet stretch belongs to the day, and isn't proof of being left. A neighbor tradition knows this question well.
The Psalms, prayed by Jews and Christians, keep the cry itself: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
Psalm 22 lets a person say it in his own voice, and further on it answers that God has not hidden his face from the one who cried. Here's the honest difference.
In the psalm, the one who feels left speaks first, and scripture keeps his cry.
In ad-Duha, the answer comes in God's voice, to the Prophet directly. The same fear, held two ways.

how: Surah ad-Duha is one of the short surahs of the Quran's last part; Muslims recite it in prayer, and some turn to it in hard seasons for its promise of not being forsaken.

o: a name for the Prophet's first night in Medina
the forenoon light of a surah that says not forsaken
the dawn prayer Muslims say before a day of fasting

games.q: the morning brightness: tap the pairs.
p: whatever came to you has left you

s: in ad-Duha, God's silence is a sign of anger
the answer: thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee.
after its comfort, ad-Duha turns to the orphan and the one who asks
so the orphan, don't oppress; the one who asks, don't drive away.
Psalm 22 and ad-Duha say exactly the same thing
the psalm keeps the cry in a person's voice; ad-Duha answers in God's voice.

games.q: a friend asks: if God is there, why do the quiet stretches happen at all? what does ad-Duha's opening oath point to?
o: night is in the oath too: the surah swears by the still night as well as the morning.
quiet stretches mean you've been abandoned; the surah confirms the fear.
the surah says no silence ever happened to the Prophet at all.
games.why: ad-Duha swears by the morning and by the still night, then says not forsaken. in the report, it came after a silence.

practice: Find the light nearest you: a window, a lamp, a patch of sky. Watch it on one surface, where it lands and where it fades into shadow. The surah swears by both, the bright morning and the still night.

wordCard.voice: The morning brightness: ad-Duha, the surah that answers a silence with not forsaken.

orig.note: Arabic: the morning brightness, the forenoon; the name of Surah 93.

carryVoice: Keep this close: not forsaken, and so, not forsaking anyone else. Three of seven from the Quran.

sources.q: Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee

sources.ref: Quran 93:1–11 (the morning hours and the still night; did He not find thee an orphan, wandering, in need; therefore the orphan, the beggar, the bounty of thy Lord)
